newsitem.title: POLAND: Pope backs Polish doctors refusing abortions.
newsitem.headline: Pope backs Polish doctors refusing abortions.

text.p: Pope John Paul on Monday praised the many Polish doctors refusing to perform abortions, an issue fiercely debated in the Pontiff's homeland.
Women's rights groups said they feared his words would heap pressure on doctors willing to carry out terminations, but who already face an intense campaign to dissuade them.
The Pope, dedicating a new heart surgery wing at a hospital in the city of Krakow, said he rejoiced that most medical staff cared for life and avoided actions leading to its destruction.
"With my whole heart I praise the doctors, nurses and all Polish health care workers who place the Divine law 'Thou shalt not kill' above what human law allows," he told hospital staff.

Poland's leftist parliament approved a law last October which allows women, after counselling, to have abortions until the 12th week of pregnancy if they cannot afford to have a child or face other personal difficulties.

This relaxed a law passed by a previous more pro-Church parliament in 1993 which allowed abortion only when pregnancy posed a threat to a woman's life, resulted from incest or rape, or the foetus had severe defects.

Wanda Nowicka, executive director of the Federation for Women and Family Planning, said a government study in January showed around half of Poland's 436 hospitals were refusing to carry out abortions for so-called social reasons.

"Medical circles are under great pressure, from the Church, local authorities and anti-choice groups, and here the Pope's words may play a role in persuading undecided doctors to stop carrying out terminations," Nowicka told Reuters.
She said in some provinces no public hospitals offered the possibility of abortions.
Nowicka said some doctors were refusing to carry out terminations in public hospitals, while agreeing to perform them privately for a hefty fee.

She added that she did not advocate forcing any doctor to carry out terminations if they had ethical reasons, but authorities should ensure at least one in every hospital was available to provide women with their rights under the law.

The clergy's tactics of putting pressure on doctors over abortion aroused fierce debate last month when bishops refused a Catholic funeral to a leading Lodz gynaecologist, Professor Waclaw Dec, who had spoken out for women's right to choose.
A military chaplain was eventually found to conduct his burial, but critics including former patients said the Church's stance had been unreasonable.

During the Pope's current 11-day pilgrimage he has repeatedly entered an abortion debate that divides Poles into two roughly equal camps and has become a major issue in campaigning for parliamentary elections due in September.
Rightist parties grouped around the pro-Church Solidarity union, which hope to supplant the ex-communists in government, say they would again restrict abortion if they won power.
"A nation which kills its own children is a nation without a future," said the Pope, head of the Roman Catholic Church which teaches that life begins at the moment of conception.

Poland's bishops have already claimed a victory from the Pope's words on abortion during the trip, saying they have helped to dissuade ex-communist President Aleksander Kwasniewski from backing a referendum on the issue.
The ruling party called for a referendum after a Polish court ruled parts of the current law unconstitutional, meaning parliament must review it within six months.
